rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers ask for a sign proving Muhammad’s prophethood or one of their proposed signs, discounting the miracles already shown to them.
rows.anchor: هلا يأتينا بآية تدل على صدقة في دعوى النبوة أو بآية من الآيات التي اقترحوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their obstinate rejection had reached the point that they no longer counted the witnessed miracles, which could make solid mountains tremble, as signs.
rows.anchor: بلغوا من المكابرة والعناد إلى حيث لم يعدوا ما شاهدوا من المعجزات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reply identifies the requested proof as the Qur’an, the greatest and most beneficial miracle: its supreme knowledge appeared through someone who had neither studied nor practiced the sciences.
rows.anchor: القرآن الكريم الذي هو أم الآيات وأس المعجزات وأرفعها وأنفعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier scriptures are the Torah, Gospel, and other revealed books; their contents are true doctrines and foundational rulings shared by all messengers.
rows.anchor: المراد بالصحف الأولى التوراة والانجيل وسائر الكتب السماوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the Qur’an a proof highlights its distinction and self-sufficient evidence; saying the proof itself came stresses its originality and suits the word bayyina.
rows.anchor: وفي إيراده بهذا العنوان ما لا يخفى من التنويه بشأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza denies their claim and the waw joins an omitted premise: other signs came, and especially this proof came, making denial impossible despite their obstinacy.
rows.anchor: والهمزة لانكار الوقوع والواو للعطف على مقدر يقتضيه المقام

rows.speaker: الإمام والطبرسي
rows.claim: Al-Imam and al-Tabarsi instead take the proof as Qur’anic accounts of earlier peoples destroyed after demanding and then rejecting signs; al-Alusi judges this interpretation unacceptable.
rows.anchor: وزعم الأمام والطبرسي أن المعنى اولم ياتهم في القرإن بيان ما

rows.speaker: أكثر السبعة وأبو بحرية وابن محيصن وطلحة وابن أبي ليلى وابن منذر وخلف وأبو عبيد وابن سعدان وابن عيسى وابن جبير الأنطاكي
rows.claim: These reciters read the verb in the proof clause with yāʾ, allowing masculine agreement because the feminine subject āya is separated from the verb.
rows.anchor: وقرأ اكثر السبعة وابو بحرية وابن محيصن وطلحة

rows.speaker: أبو زيد عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Zayd’s report from Abu Amr reads bayyinatin with tanwīn and treats mā as its appositive substitute.
rows.anchor: أبو زيد عن أبي عمرو ( بينة ) بالتنوين على أن ما بدل

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: The author of al-Lawāmiḥ allows mā to be negative on this reading, referring to Qur’anic abrogating material and merit absent from previous books; al-Alusi dismisses this proposal.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب اللوامح : يجوز أن تكون ما على هذه القراءة نافية

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group reads bayyinatan with accusative and tanwīn, construing it as a circumstantial accusative and mā as the subject.
rows.anchor: بنصب ( بينة ) والتنوين على أنه حال وما فاعل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to read al-ṣuḥuf with a sukūn on ḥāʾ for ease of pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة منهم ابن عباس الصحف باسكان الحاء للتخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each side, believers and disbelievers, awaits the outcome of its affair; mutarabbis is the predicate of kull and is singular to match kull’s grammatical form.
rows.anchor: أي منتظر لما يؤل اليه أمرنا وأمركم وهو خبر كل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reading has fa-tamattaʿū in place of fa-tarabbaṣū.
rows.anchor: وقرئ فتمتعوا ( فستعلمون ( عن قريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-sawī means straight; the promised outcome will show who possesses the straight path and who is guided from error.
rows.anchor: أي المستقيم وقرأ أبو مجلز وعمران بن حدير

rows.speaker: أبو مجلز وعمران بن حدير
rows.claim: Abu Mujliz and Imran ibn Hudayr read al-siwāʾ, meaning the middle or excellent path.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو مجلز وعمران بن حدير ( السواء ) أي الوسط

rows.speaker: الجحدري وابن يعمر
rows.claim: Al-Jaḥdarī and Ibn Yaʿmar read al-sūʾā, a feminine form of al-aswaʾ, with feminine agreement because ṣirāṭ may be feminine.
rows.anchor: بالضم والقصر على وزن فعلى وهو تأنيث الاسوا وأنث لتأنيث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reads al-sūʾ, meaning evil.
rows.anchor: رضى الله تعالى عنهما ( السوء ) بفتح وسكون وهمزة آخره

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: For the variant al-suyy with doubled yāʾ, Abu Hayyan prefers deriving it as a diminutive of sawāʾ, like ʿaṭā becoming ʿaṭiyy, because a diminutive of the proposed form should retain its hamza.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان : الاجود أن يكون تصغير سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reports the objection that exchanging the hamza for yāʾ is permissible, and another al-suyy reading with doubled wāw is explained as a softened al-sūʾā.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن إبدال مثل هذه الهمزة ياء جائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-man ihtadā means whoever was guided out of error; the comparison implicit in this wording is absent in the majority reading and in the first anomalous reading.
rows.anchor: أي من الضلالة ولم تراع على قراءة الجمهور

words: من أصحاب الصراط السوي ومن اهتدى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the main parsing, both man clauses are interrogative subjects with following predicates; together they fill the suspended verb’s two objects, or its one object if ʿalima means to know.
rows.anchor: ومن في الموضعين استفهامية في محل رفع على الأبتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second man may be relative and coordinate with the first interrogative clause if ʿalima means to know; otherwise coordination would leave an impermissibly omitted object.
rows.anchor: وجوز كون من الثانية موصولة فتكون معطوفة على محل

words: من أصحاب الصراط السوي ومن اهتدى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the second clause can coordinate with aṣḥāb or ṣirāṭ, asking who is guided or who belongs to the guided one’s path; if both refer to the Prophet, the coordination joins descriptions of one person.
rows.anchor: فتكون في حيز من الاستفهامية أي ومن الذي اهتدى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ permits the first man to be a relative pronoun functioning as the object of ʿilm, with aṣḥāb as the predicate of an elided subject; Kūfans allow omission of this relative pronoun, unlike Basrans.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الفراء أن تكون من الأولى موصولة أيضا بمعنى الذين

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi sees the ending as answering the opening: after bearing the burden of proclamation without exhausting oneself, the Prophet should worship within his capacity and leave those whom warning will not benefit; they will regret their opposition.
rows.anchor: وما أشد مناسبة هذه الخاتمة للفاتحة وقد ذكر الطيبي انها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An inward reading says Moses feared that God had clothed the magicians’ sorcery in the garment of overpowering; only the doomed feel secure from God’s plan.
rows.anchor: إنه عليه السلام رأى أن الله تعالى البس سحر السحرة

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says Moses feared for his people lest they lose their share of God, not for himself; “you are uppermost” means either guarded by divine care or victorious enough to make them followers.
rows.anchor: وسئل ابن عطاء عن ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magicians’ prostration shows that God may grant guidance and arrival to Him very quickly; recent penitents can attain spiritual perfection, despite ignorant critics’ disbelief.
rows.anchor: فيه إشارة إلى أن الله تعالى يمن على من يشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magicians’ refusal expresses the high aspiration produced by certainty: eternal spiritual bliss outweighs worldly happiness, bodily suffering, immediate pleasure, and physical pain.
rows.anchor: كلام صادر من عظم الهمة الحاصل للنفس بقوة اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to travel by night signifies the desirability of leaving distractions and avoiding company with wicked people.
rows.anchor: فيه اشارة إلى استحباب مفارقة الأغيار وترك صحبة الاشرار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here transgression means using a blessing heedlessly and without intending to employ it in obedience to God.
rows.anchor: عد من الطغيان فيه استعماله مع الغفلة عن الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage teaches a leader to choose what is best for followers and a person not to act in a way that invites a disciple’s suspicion, especially when the disciple is ungrounded.
rows.anchor: الأشارة فيه أنه ينبغي للرئيس رعاية الأصلح في حق المرؤس

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says God told Moses he brought the trial on by telling Aaron to succeed him without entrusting the succession to God and relying on Him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطاء : إن الله تعالى قال لموسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say God disclosed the trial to Moses to show intimacy and occupy him with divine companionship instead of the company of adversaries; al-Alusi dismisses this explanation.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم أن سر اخبار الله تعالى إياه بما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Samiri became the cause of the people’s misguidance through what he fashioned.
rows.anchor: صار سبب ضلالهم بما صنع

rows.speaker: some interpreters
rows.claim: A Sufi interpretation says the trial distinguished those ready for perfection through detachment from those immersed in matter, limited to sense and unable to notice immaterial realities.
rows.anchor: قال بعض أهل التأويل : إنما ابتلاهم الله تعالى بما ابتلاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their phrase means they did not break the promise by their own power: as natural servants they have no independent judgment or mastery and follow imitation and practice, not verification and knowledge.
rows.anchor: أي برأينا فانهم عبيد بالطبع لا رأى لهم ولا ملكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Samiri enslaved them through an astral talisman made from ornaments because their lower, bodily natures were deeply attached to gold and naturally adorned the form through affinity.
rows.anchor: وإنما استعبدهم السامري بالطلسم المفرغ من الحلي لرسوخ محبة الذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The talisman is interpreted as mixing heavenly forces—the effect of the universal animal soul, symbolized by Ḥayẓūm and Gabriel’s mount—with earthly forces; Gabriel’s mount symbolizes the active intellect.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك من باب مزج القوى السماوية التي هي اثر النفس الحيوانية الكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Samiri’s claim to perceive what others did not is read as knowledge of natural and mathematical sciences, the basis of talismans and simiyāʾ.
rows.anchor: أي من العلم الطبيعي والرياضي اللذين يبنى عليهما علم الطلسمات والسيمياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ angry command exiled the Samiri; those angered by prophets or saints, as manifestations of divine attributes, fall under God’s power and suffer in both worlds, and the no-contact punishment reflects the Samiri’s distance from truth and Moses’ curse.
rows.anchor: غضبا على السامري وطردا له وكل من غضب عليه الأنبياء

rows.speaker: أهل الوحدة
rows.claim: The people of unity read the mountains as all existent things, which divine effusions from the source of oneness sweep away at the great resurrection into flat, single existence without duality or otherness.
rows.anchor: قال أهل الوحدة : أي يسألونك عن موجودات الأشياء

rows.speaker: أهل الوحدة
rows.claim: In that reading, all follow God as caller without deviation because God holds their forelocks and alone acts; voices are humbled, with whispering understood as a hidden command relative to manifestations.
rows.anchor: يومئذ يتبعون الداعي الذي هو الحق سبحانه لا عوج له

rows.speaker: some interpreters
rows.claim: An inward explanation identifies the one permitted to intercede as someone who has purified action and belief, attributes no deed to self, and recognizes no independent agency.
rows.anchor: قيل : هو من صحح فعله وعقده ولم ينسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s transcendence makes Him inaccessible to complete intellectual grasp; people differ in knowledge of His attributes according to their capacities, the knowledge alluded to in the prayer for increase in knowledge.
rows.anchor: لكمال تقدسه وتنزهه وجلاله سبحانه عز وجل فهيهات أن تحلق

rows.speaker: some interpreters
rows.claim: Some take the prayer for increased knowledge as an allusion to knowledge bestowed directly by God.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هذا إشارة إلى العلم اللدني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam’s story warns people to be especially cautious of disobedience; a cited poem rebukes those who commit sins yet expect paradise, recalling that one sin led to Adam’s expulsion.
rows.anchor: والأشارة في قصة آدم عليه السلام إلى أنه ينبغي للانسان

rows.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits from Ibn Abbas that Adam wept after his expulsion and Gabriel wept with him; God reminded Adam of his blessings, command, and disobedience, then said mercy had preceded wrath, accepted his supplication, and forgave him.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس قال : بينا إدم عليه السلام يبكي جاءه جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poem rebukes those who pile up sins yet hope to reach paradise, reminding them that Adam was sent from it after a single sin.
rows.anchor: تصل الذنوب إلى الذنوب وترتجي درج الجنان بها وفوز العابد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning away from remembrance means turning toward the lower world; material attraction and greed produce a constricted life through obsessive attachment to possessions and miserliness.
rows.anchor: أي بالتوجه إلى العالم السفلى

rows.speaker: some interpreters
rows.claim: Some say that turning from remembrance darkens one’s time and disrupts one’s livelihood, while remembrance brings certainty and trust, ease, generosity with what one has, and contentment with what one lacks.
rows.anchor: لا يعرض أحد عن ذكر ربه سبحانه إلا اظلم عليه وقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worthy final outcome belongs to people of spiritual strength who shed psychic vices and acquire spiritual virtues.
rows.anchor: العاقبة التي تعتبر وتستاهل أن تسمى عاقبة لأهل القوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ is Meccan according to a report from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr and, without disagreement, according to al-Baḥr; the source records an exception at 21:44.
rows.anchor: نزلت بمكة كما أخرج ابن مردوية عن ابن عباس وابن الزبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source records 21:44 as the verse excepted from the sūra’s Meccan classification.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى ( أفلا ترون أنا نأتي الأرض )

rows.speaker: الطبرسي والداني
rows.claim: Al-Tabarsi and al-Dani count the sūra as 112 verses in the Kufan count and 111 in the other counts.
rows.anchor: وهي مائة واثنتا عشرة آية في عد الكوفي وإحدى عشرة في عد الباقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The connection of Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ to the preceding sūra is self-evident.
rows.anchor: ووجه اتصالهما بما قبلهما غني عن البيان

rows.speaker: عامر بن ربيعة
rows.claim: Amir ibn Rabiʿa relates that an Arab guest offered him part of a valley he had asked the Prophet to grant, but Amir declined because the newly revealed sūra had distracted them from worldly concerns; al-Alusi cites Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and Ibn ʿAsakir.
rows.anchor: عن عامر ابن ربيعة أنه نزل به رجل من العرب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains the sky’s protection as preservation from decay and alteration over the long duration of the world; this does not conflict with its eventual folding and destruction at the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: من البلى والتغير على طول الدهر كما روي عن قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the sky is protected from falling.
rows.anchor: وقيل : من الوقوع وقال الفراء : من استراق السمع بالرجوم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains the protection as shielding the sky from the devils’ eavesdropping, by means of shooting stars.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : من استراق السمع بالرجوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi objects that protection from eavesdropping makes mention of a roof seem pointless; the proposed answer is that earthly roofs can be climbed by thieves, unlike the sky.
rows.anchor: أنه يكون ذكر السقف لغوا لا يناسب البلاغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation is that the sky is protected from those beneath it, which in turn indicates complete protection for them from the sky.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه للدلالة على حفظها عمن تحتها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas relates that the Prophet looked at the sky and called it a raised roof and restrained wave that runs like an arrow and is protected from devils; if sound, the report is not explicit proof of the verse’s meaning, contrary to Abu Hayyan’s claim.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما قال : أن رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the sky is protected from idolatry and sins, but the author says the same objection applies as to the preceding interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل : من الشرك والمعاصي ويرد عليه ما أورد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky’s signs indicate God’s oneness, knowledge, wisdom, power, and will; some are as evident as the sun, while others emerge through investigation.
rows.anchor: الدالة على وحدانيتنا وعلمنا وحكمنا وقدرتنا وإرادتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those turning away are heedless of the signs and do not seriously consider them through the lens of faith.
rows.anchor: ذاهلون عنها لا يجيلون قداح الكفر فيها

rows.speaker: مجاهد وحميد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Humayd read āyatihā in the singular: each thing in the sky suffices as a sign; on this reading, turning away means denying that it clearly proves a Creator.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وحميد ( عن آيتها بالإفراد ووجه بأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun and moon are the signs of night and day; their mention illustrates the preceding signs, with a shift of address that emphasizes the discourse’s point.
rows.anchor: اللذين هما آيتاهما ولذا لم يعد الفعل بيانا لبعض تلك الآيات

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some explain the choice of jaʿala for the sky and khalaqa here by saying night and day are not produced like animals or mountains; al-Alusi calls this explanation unconvincing.
rows.anchor: ولما كان إيجاد الليل والنهار ليس على نمط إيجاد الحيوانات وإيجاد الرواسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kull is the subject, with its tanwīn standing in for a genitive complement; al-Zamakhshari takes the implied complement as the singular indefinite “each one of the sun and moon.”
rows.anchor: مبتدأ وتنوينه عوض عن المضاف إليه واعتبره صاحب الكشاف

rows.speaker: ابن هشام
rows.claim: Ibn Hisham objects that if kull’s omitted complement is singular indefinite, its agreeing pronoun must also be singular; the plural verb instead requires construing the complement as a plural definite, with agreement revealing the omitted form.
rows.anchor: قد صرح ابن هشام في المغنى بأن المقدر إذا كان مفردا نكرة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan allows either singular or plural agreement regardless of how the omitted complement of kull is construed, permitting al-Zamakhshari’s analysis.
rows.anchor: وأبو حيان يجوز الإفراد والجمع مطلقا فيجوز هنا اعتبار المضاف إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fī falak is the predicate; its singular form suits kull’s distributive, indefinite sense of each one, rather than a collective sense.
rows.anchor: خبره ووجه إفراده ظاهر لأن النكرة المقدرة للعموم البدلي لا الشمولي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If kull is taken as a plural generic, the phrase means each belongs to its own orbit, since sun and moon do not together occupy one orbit.
rows.anchor: ومن قدر جمعا معرفا قال : المراد به الجنس الكلي المؤل بالجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yasbaḥūn may be a circumstantial clause or a predicate, with fī falak then functioning circumstantially or as its complement; the whole kull clause can modify sun and moon without a conjunction, or be taken as a new sentence.
rows.anchor: حال ويجوز أن يكون الخبر و ( في فلك ) حالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural pronoun can reflect the many apparent rising points of the sun and moon, allowing figurative plural forms despite one of each in reality.
rows.anchor: وكان ضميرهما جمعا اعتبارا للتكثير بتكاثر المطالع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says the two luminaries receive a plural pronoun by honorific precedence; others take it to refer to stars, or also to sun, moon, night, and day, though the latter is unsuitable because night and day do not swim even figuratively.
rows.anchor: وفيه أن الليل والنهار لا يحسن وصفهما بالسباحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rational plural agreement is explained either by the view of some Muslims that the celestial bodies are actually rational or by treating them as rational because swimming is normally an act of rational agents.
rows.anchor: واختيار ضمير العقلاء إما لأنهما عقلاء حقيقية كما ذهب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
rows.claim: Falak originally denotes any round, revolving object, as in the spindle’s whorl; Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi identify the orbit here as the heaven.
rows.anchor: والفلك في الأصل كل شيء دائر ومنه فلكه المغزل

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the falak as a contained wave beneath the heaven in which the sun and moon travel.
rows.anchor: وقال أكثر المفسرين : هو موج مكفوف تحت السماء

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the falak is not a body but the orbit of the stars.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك : هو ليس بجسم وإنما هو مدار هذه النجوم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
rows.claim: The well-known transmitted interpretation from Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi is that falak means heaven, implying that heaven is spherical; al-Alusi finds a subtle hint of this in the distributive wording, and says its being a roof does not rule it out.
rows.anchor: والمشهور ما روي عن ابن عباس والسدي وفيه القول باستدارة السماء

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: Philosophers describe each celestial sphere as living, knowing, volitionally moving only in a circle, imperishable, indivisible, and without the ordinary elemental qualities or tendencies.
rows.anchor: في كلام الفلاسفة إطلاق الفلك على السماء ووصوفه بأنه حي عالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalam theologians reject many of these philosophical claims; philosophers infer multiple spheres from the impossibility of celestial rupture and differing planetary motions, and commonly posit nine in all.
rows.anchor: وقد رد ذلك في الكتب الكلامية وبنوا على امتناع الخرق والالتئام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard philosophical scheme assigns seven spheres to the wandering planets, one to fixed stars, and one outer sphere to impart daily motion to all.
rows.anchor: والمشهور أن الأفلاك الكلية تسعة سبعة للسبع السيارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says there is no decisive proof that no additional spheres exist; even Avicenna was unsure whether fixed stars occupy one sphere or nested spheres.
rows.anchor: والحق أنه لا قاطع على نفي ما عدا ذلك ألا ترى أن الشيخ الرئيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that similar apparent stellar motions prove the stars occupy one sphere is uncertain: observations may conceal tiny differences, such as rotations taking 36,000 years versus slightly less.
rows.anchor: وقولهم إن حركات الثوابت متشابهة ومتى كانت كذلك كانت مركوزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source adds that later astronomers found Herschel, whose motion is faster than the fixed stars’ but slower than the visible planets’, unknown to earlier observers.
rows.anchor: وجدان المتأخرين من أهل الأرصاد كوكبا أسرع حركة من الثوابت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inference that objects with similar motions share one sphere is not conclusive, since distinct things can share properties; separate spheres could move in the same direction and share poles and other dimensions.
rows.anchor: وأما كبراه فلا احتمال اشتراك الأشياء المختلفة في كثير من اللوازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Additional spheres could lie between planetary spheres; the geometric objection based on equal nearest and farthest distances fails because epicycles and the lunar node sphere can intervene.
rows.anchor: بل حاصل في كل الأفلاك فيجوز أن يكون بين أفلاك السيارة أفلاك أخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Astronomers posit several epicycle spheres for each superior planet and five for inferior planets; assuming adjacent spheres touch because no interposed sphere exists is circular, so another proof is needed.
rows.anchor: ذكر المحققون من أصحاب الهيئة أن لفلك التدوير لكل من العلوية
